evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by CD spectroscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: A search for the helicase interaction motif within the Bacillus subtilis proteome using PROSITE with the query [VIL]-D-X-X-T-G-E-[VIL]-[VILT] retrieved seven proteins.
source: To investigate whether the helicase interaction motif we had identified in RpoB played a wider role in mediating PcrA interactions, we searched for it within the Bacillus subtilis proteome using PROSITE with the query [VIL]-D-X-X-T-G-E-[VIL]-[VILT], where X is any amino acid and the square brackets indicate ambiguity. This search retrieved seven proteins (only ~0.3 are expected by chance), four of which (RpoB, UvrB, YxaL, and YwhK) are known to interact with PcrA (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Four of the seven proteins retrieved by the motif search (RpoB, UvrB, YxaL, and YwhK) are known to interact with PcrA.
source: This search retrieved seven proteins (only ~0.3 are expected by chance), four of which (RpoB, UvrB, YxaL, and YwhK) are known to interact with PcrA (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The structure of UvrB and high-confidence homology models of YxaL and YwhK all show that the conserved TGE triad is located at the tip of a surface loop flanked by β sheets.
source: Importantly, the structure of UvrB and high-confidence homology models of YxaL and YwhK all show that, as is the case for the beta subunit of E. coli RNAP, the conserved TGE triad is located at the tip of a surface loop flanked by β sheets (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: When the motif search was applied more broadly across the entire SwissProt database it returned only 607 sequences, of which 326 and 42 were bacterial RpoB and UvrB sequences respectively.
source: When this same motif search was applied more broadly across the entire SwissProt database it returned only 607 sequences, of which 326 and 42 were bacterial RpoB and UvrB sequences respectively, demonstrating its very high specificity for returning PcrA interactors.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by bioinformatic analysis.

claim: The motif search demonstrates very high specificity for returning PcrA interactors.
source: When this same motif search was applied more broadly across the entire SwissProt database it returned only 607 sequences, of which 326 and 42 were bacterial RpoB and UvrB sequences respectively, demonstrating its very high specificity for returning PcrA interactors.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the Results section based on the bioinformatic analysis.

claim: YxaL and YwhK are β propeller proteins that have been identified as PcrA interactors using yeast two-hybrid and biochemical assays.
source: YxaL and YwhK are β propeller proteins that have been identified as PcrA interactors using yeast two-hybrid and biochemical assays (Noirot-Gros et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: The fragment of YxaL found to interact with PcrA in the yeast two-hybrid assay is consistent with the location of the newly identified motif.
source: The fragment of YxaL found to interact with PcrA in the yeast two-hybrid assay is consistent with the location of the newly identified motif.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section based on comparison with previous yeast two-hybrid data.

claim: UvrB has already been shown to bind to the C-terminal domain of E. coli UvrD.
source: Importantly, UvrB has already been shown to bind to the C-terminal domain of E. coli UvrD (Manelyte et al., 2009) and this interaction is, therefore, potentially analogous to that formed between the CTD and RNAP β.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: The interaction between UvrB and the C-terminal domain of E. coli UvrD is potentially analogous to that formed between the CTD and RNAP β.
source: Importantly, UvrB has already been shown to bind to the C-terminal domain of E. coli UvrD (Manelyte et al., 2009) and this interaction is, therefore, potentially analogous to that formed between the CTD and RNAP β.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the Results section based on the similarity of the interaction motifs.

claim: Substitution of the glutamic acid in the UvrB TGE motif (E233) severely disrupted the interaction with PcrA.
source: To validate the predicted PcrA binding site on UvrB, we performed pulldown experiments using his-tagged UvrB as bait and myc-tagged PcrA in B. subtilis extracts as prey (Figure 3C). These experiments confirmed the expected interaction between PcrA and wild-type UvrB protein. Furthermore, and in agreement with our hypothesis, substitution of the glutamic acid in the UvrB TGE motif (E233) severely disrupted the interaction with PcrA while having no effect on the DNA-stimulated ATPase activity of UvrB (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by pulldown data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Substitution of the glutamic acid in the UvrB TGE motif (E233) had no effect on the DNA-stimulated ATPase activity of UvrB.
source: Furthermore, and in agreement with our hypothesis, substitution of the glutamic acid in the UvrB TGE motif (E233) severely disrupted the interaction with PcrA while having no effect on the DNA-stimulated ATPase activity of UvrB (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by ATPase assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The PcrA interaction motif is located within domain 2 of UvrB, which also interacts with UvrA.
source: Inspection of the domain architecture of UvrB reveals that the PcrA interaction motif is located within domain 2, which also interacts with UvrA (Pakotiprapha et al., 2012; Truglio et al., 2004; Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and citations.

claim: Because amino acid substitutions reported to disrupt UvrA-UvrB interaction are not within the motif itself, binding of UvrA to UvrB would not necessarily preclude binding of PcrA/UvrD.
source: However, because amino acid substitutions reported to disrupt UvrA-UvrB interaction are not within the motif itself, binding of UvrA to UvrB would not necessarily preclude binding of PcrA/UvrD.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the Results section based on the location of the motif and previous mutagenesis data.

claim: A high scoring docking model for the interaction between the PcrA-CTD and UvrB using HADDOCK suggests that the complex is stabilised by an electrostatic interaction between UvrB E233 and the PcrA K727 residue.
source: Interestingly, a high scoring docking model for the interaction between the PcrA-CTD and UvrB using HADDOCK (van Zundert et al., 2016) suggests that the complex is stabilised by an electrostatic interaction between UvrB E233 and the PcrA K727 residue, which is known to be critical for interaction between PcrA and RNAP (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by docking analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: PcrA K727 residue is known to be critical for interaction between PcrA and RNAP.
source: Interestingly, a high scoring docking model for the interaction between the PcrA-CTD and UvrB using HADDOCK (van Zundert et al., 2016) suggests that the complex is stabilised by an electrostatic interaction between UvrB E233 and the PcrA K727 residue, which is known to be critical for interaction between PcrA and RNAP (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Results section.

claim: The docked complex shows how PcrA might be recruited to sites of damage after the damaged oligonucleotide has been nicked, as DNA near the docking site is accessible.
source: The docked complex shows how PcrA might be recruited to sites of damage after the damaged oligonucleotide has been nicked, as DNA near the docking site is accessible.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the Results section based on the docking model.

claim: The interaction between the PcrA C-terminal Tudor domain and UvrB is equivalent in molecular terms to its interaction with RNA polymerase.
source: Our results predict that the interaction between the PcrA C-terminal Tudor domain and UvrB is equivalent in molecular terms to its interaction with RNA polymerase.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the Results section based on the similarity of the interaction motifs and pulldown data.

claim: UvrB and RNA polymerase might be engaged in a simple competition for the Tudor domain of PcrA.
source: A corollary is that UvrB and RNA polymerase might be engaged in a simple competition for the Tudor domain of PcrA.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the Results section based on the similarity of the interaction motifs.

claim: Introduction of UvrB significantly reduced the amount of RNA polymerase that was recovered from the cell extract in pulldown experiments using PcrA as a bait.
source: To test this, we performed pulldown of RNA polymerase using PcrA as a bait and titrated the cell extract (i.e. the prey proteins) with increasing concentrations of purified recombinant UvrB (Figure 3D–E). As expected, introduction of UvrB significantly reduced the amount of RNA polymerase that was recovered from the cell extract.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by pulldown data shown in Figure 3D–E.

claim: Titration of free Mfd did not diminish the yield of RNAP in pulldown assays using PcrA as a bait.
source: As has been noted previously, other RNAP interactors also bind to the RpoB subunit via Tudor domains, including the transcription-repair coupling factor Mfd. Interestingly, using the same pulldown assay, titration of free Mfd did not diminish the yield of RNAP (Figure 3D–E), despite biotinylated Mfd pulling down RNAP subunits under similar conditions (Table 2).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by pulldown data shown in Figure 3D–E.

claim: Biotinylated Mfd pulls down RNAP subunits under similar conditions.
source: Interestingly, using the same pulldown assay, titration of free Mfd did not diminish the yield of RNAP (Figure 3D–E), despite biotinylated Mfd pulling down RNAP subunits under similar conditions (Table 2).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by pulldown data shown in Table 2.

claim: Although both PcrA and Mfd contain Tudor domains for interaction with RNAP, they bind at different physical locations and without competing.
source: This suggests that, although both proteins contain Tudor domains for interaction with RNAP, PcrA, and Mfd bind at different physical locations and without competing.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the Results section based on the pulldown data.

claim: The observation that PcrA and Mfd bind at different physical locations is in agreement with recently-published observations for the E. coli system.
source: This is in agreement with recently-published observations for the E. coli system (Kawale and Burmann, 2020), as well as the lack of protection of the expected Mfd-interacting region of RpoB (the β1 domain) that we observe in our HDX experiments (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; Smith and Savery, 2005; Westblade et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations and HDX-MS data.

claim: The lack of protection of the expected Mfd-interacting region of RpoB (the β1 domain) in HDX experiments is consistent with PcrA and Mfd binding at different physical locations.
source: This is in agreement with recently-published observations for the E. coli system (Kawale and Burmann, 2020), as well as the lack of protection of the expected Mfd-interacting region of RpoB (the β1 domain) that we observe in our HDX experiments (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; Smith and Savery, 2005; Westblade et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Previous work in live E. coli and B. subtilis cells has found at most mild phenotypes associated with deletion of the C-terminal domain of UvrD and PcrA, respectively.
source: Despite the apparently critical role played by the CTD in RNAP interactions, previous work in live E. coli and B. subtilis cells has found at most mild phenotypes associated with deletion of the C-terminal domain of UvrD and PcrA, respectively (Manelyte et al., 2009; Merrikh et al., 2015; Sanders et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: The N-terminal region of PcrA, including the helicase core, also contributes significantly to the interaction with RNA polymerase.
source: This led us to consider the possibility that the N-terminal region of PcrA, including the helicase core, also contributes significantly to the interaction with RNA polymerase.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the Results section based on the mild phenotypes of CTD deletion.

claim: Crosslinking studies of UvrD-RNAP implicated the 1B and 2B subdomains of UvrD in interactions with the RNAP β-flap tip and the N-terminal region of the β′ subunit.
source: This view is consistent with crosslinking studies of UvrD-RNAP which implicated the 1B and 2B subdomains of UvrD in interactions with the RNAP β-flap tip and the N-terminal region of the β′ subunit (Epshtein et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: The RNAP β-flap tip and the N-terminal region of the β′ subunit surround the RNA and DNA exit channels.
source: Note that these structural features surround the RNA and DNA exit channels.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Results section.

claim: The interaction between PcrA-ΔCTD and RNAP was barely detected by pulldown/proteomics experiments in vitro (Kd > 1.5 µM).
source: We did not pursue HDX experiments between PcrA-ΔCTD and RNAP because our previous work had shown that this interaction was barely detected by pulldown/proteomics experiments in vitro (Gwynn et al., 2013; Sanders et al., 2017) even with the favoured TEC substrate (Kd > 1.5 µM; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Results section and supported by citations and EMSA data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: PcrA showed HDX protection in two main regions upon interaction with RNAP: the 2A domain and the CTD.
source: PcrA showed HDX protection in two main regions upon interaction with RNAP: the 2A domain and the CTD (blue and magenta highlights respectively; Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Peptides from the long flexible linker between the 2A domain and the CTD were not detected above the confidence threshold in HDX-MS experiments.
source: Note that peptides from the long flexible linker between these two regions were not detected above the confidence threshold and so we have no data for that part of the protein.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a limitation of the HDX-MS data.

claim: Most of the protected regions outside of the CTD prominently cluster in the 2A domain and on the side of the helicase which also binds to DNA.
source: Most of the protected regions outside of the CTD prominently cluster in the 2A domain and on the side of the helicase which also binds to DNA.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The crosslinking positions identified in domains 1B and 2B in previous work are on the same DNA-facing side of the helicase and are broadly consistent with the HDX-MS data.
source: The crosslinking positions identified in domains 1B and 2B in previous work are on the same DNA-facing side of the helicase and are therefore broadly consistent with these data (Epshtein et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by comparison with previous crosslinking data.

claim: The HDX protection afforded to the RNAP subunits in the presence of full length PcrA was more extensive than in the presence of the CTD.
source: The HDX protection afforded to the RNAP subunits in the presence of full length PcrA was more extensive than in the presence of the CTD, and identified important regions in the two largest subunits, β and β′ (butterfly plots for the rest of the subunits are shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: In agreement with data for the CTD-RNAP interaction, the SI1 region showed protection that is assigned to the interaction with the PcrA Tudor domain.
source: In agreement with our data for the CTD-RNAP interaction, the SI1 region showed protection that we therefore assign to the interaction with the PcrA Tudor domain (Figure 5A, green shadow and Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The other protected region within the β subunit corresponds to the β flap tip, as identified by crosslinking in the E. coli system.
source: The other protected region within the β subunit corresponds to the β flap tip, as identified by crosslinking in the E. coli system (Epshtein et al., 2014; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and comparison with previous crosslinking data.

claim: The β′ subunit showed two protected clusters in the N-terminal and central regions.
source: The β′ subunit also showed two protected clusters in the N-terminal and central regions (Figure 5B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Protected regions of RNAP surround the RNA and DNA exit channels.
source: The recent structure of the B. subtilis transcription elongation complex allowed us to visualise the results (Newing et al., 2020; Figure 5C) and reveals that protected regions of RNAP surround the RNA and DNA exit channels.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by HDX-MS data visualized on the structure shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The zinc finger domain of the β′ subunit was not covered by the HDX-MS dataset.
source: Unfortunately, the zinc finger domain of the β′ subunit was not covered by our dataset but, given its close proximity to the protected regions we have observed, as well as the crosslinking analysis of the E. coli RNAP-UvrD complex (Epshtein et al., 2014), it is likely to be involved in the interaction too.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a limitation of the HDX-MS data.

claim: Given the close proximity of the zinc finger domain to the protected regions and the crosslinking analysis of the E. coli RNAP-UvrD complex, it is likely to be involved in the interaction too.
source: Unfortunately, the zinc finger domain of the β′ subunit was not covered by our dataset but, given its close proximity to the protected regions we have observed, as well as the crosslinking analysis of the E. coli RNAP-UvrD complex (Epshtein et al., 2014), it is likely to be involved in the interaction too.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the Results section based on the proximity of the zinc finger domain to protected regions and previous crosslinking data.

claim: The HDX-MS data suggested that the PcrA helicase might be acting close to the RNA and DNA exit channels.
source: Taken together, our data suggested to us that the PcrA helicase might be acting close to the RNA and DNA exit channels and are consistent with our earlier conclusion that Mfd and PcrA bind to different parts of RNAP.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the Results section based on the HDX-MS data.

claim: The HDX-MS data are consistent with the conclusion that Mfd and PcrA bind to different parts of RNAP.
source: Taken together, our data suggested to us that the PcrA helicase might be acting close to the RNA and DNA exit channels and are consistent with our earlier conclusion that Mfd and PcrA bind to different parts of RNAP.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the HDX-MS data.

claim: PcrA/UvrD is a 3′>5′ ssDNA translocase and helicase that binds preferentially to 3′-ssDNA overhangs to initiate unwinding of flanking DNA duplexes.
source: It is well established that PcrA/UvrD is a 3′>5′ ssDNA translocase and helicase that binds preferentially to 3′-ssDNA overhangs to initiate unwinding of flanking DNA duplexes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Results section.

claim: UvrD has been shown to unwind DNA-RNA hybrids efficiently.
source: However, UvrD has also been shown to unwind DNA-RNA hybrids efficiently (Matson, 1989), although we are not aware of a cellular function having been ascribed to this activity.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: A cellular function has not been ascribed to the DNA-RNA hybrid unwinding activity of UvrD.
source: However, UvrD has also been shown to unwind DNA-RNA hybrids efficiently (Matson, 1989), although we are not aware of a cellular function having been ascribed to this activity.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge in the Results section.

claim: No data is available for the enzyme's activity on RNA duplexes.
source: Moreover, no data is available for the enzyme's activity on RNA duplexes.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge in the Results section.

claim: PcrA was able to efficiently unwind the two substrates in which the 3′-ssDNA tail was formed from DNA, including an all-DNA duplex and a DNA-RNA hybrid.
source: PcrA was able to efficiently unwind the two substrates in which the 3′-ssDNA tail was formed from DNA, including an all-DNA duplex and a DNA-RNA hybrid (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by helicase assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: PcrA was unable to unwind either substrate containing a 3′-ssRNA tail (either an RNA-DNA hybrid or an RNA duplex), even at elevated concentrations.
source: In contrast, the enzyme was unable to unwind either substrate containing a 3′-ssRNA tail (either an RNA-DNA hybrid or an RNA duplex), even at elevated concentrations.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by helicase assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Unwinding of both the DNA duplex and the RNA-DNA hybrid was absolutely dependent on the presence of the 3′-ssDNA tail.
source: Unwinding of both the DNA duplex and the RNA-DNA hybrid was absolutely dependent on the presence of the 3′-ssDNA tail (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B), implying that it is initiated by enzymes binding to ssDNA and moving in the 3′>5′ direction.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by helicase assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: Unwinding is initiated by enzymes binding to ssDNA and moving in the 3′>5′ direction.
source: Unwinding of both the DNA duplex and the RNA-DNA hybrid was absolutely dependent on the presence of the 3′-ssDNA tail (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B), implying that it is initiated by enzymes binding to ssDNA and moving in the 3′>5′ direction.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the Results section based on the helicase assay data.

claim: In the absence of DNA or RNA, the basal ATPase activity of PcrA was low (~1 s−1).
source: In the absence of DNA or RNA, the basal ATPase activity of PcrA was low (~1 s−1).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by ATPase assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The ATPase activity of PcrA was stimulated approximately 100-fold in the presence of poly(dT) single-stranded DNA.
source: However, it was stimulated approximately 100-fold in the presence of poly(dT) single-stranded DNA.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by ATPase assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Poly(U) single-stranded RNA had no effect on the observed ATPase activity of PcrA.
source: In contrast, poly(U) single-stranded RNA had no effect on the observed ATPase activity.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by ATPase assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: PcrA helicase can efficiently unwind DNA-RNA hybrids but can only do so by ATP-dependent translocation on the DNA strand.
source: These experiments demonstrate that PcrA helicase can efficiently unwind DNA-RNA hybrids but can only do so by ATP-dependent translocation on the DNA strand.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the helicase and ATPase assay data.

claim: PcrA might act to unwind R-loops formed during transcription.
source: Together with the HDX experiments localising PcrA to the RNA and DNA exit channels, we hypothesised that PcrA might act to unwind R-loops formed during transcription.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the Results section based on the helicase assay data and HDX-MS data.

claim: Both PcrA and UvrD have been shown to interact with RNAP and to alleviate replication-transcription conflicts (in B. subtilis and E. coli, respectively).
source: Both PcrA and UvrD have been shown to interact with RNAP and to alleviate replication-transcription conflicts (in B. subtilis and E. coli, respectively) (Guy et al., 2009; Hawkins et al., 2019; Merrikh et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: The precise role for the PcrA/UvrD-RNAP interaction remains unknown.
source: However, the precise role for this interaction remains unknown and study of the system is frustrated by the essentiality of both PcrA and RNA polymerase, making phenotypic analysis more complex.

claim: Study of the PcrA/UvrD-RNAP system is frustrated by the essentiality of both PcrA and RNA polymerase, making phenotypic analysis more complex.
source: However, the precise role for this interaction remains unknown and study of the system is frustrated by the essentiality of both PcrA and RNA polymerase, making phenotypic analysis more complex.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a challenge in studying the system.

claim: A dominant negative mutant of PcrA/UvrD in which a glutamate in the Walker B motif is substituted allows DNA and ATP binding, but not hydrolysis and concomitant DNA translocation.
source: To overcome this difficulty, we first exploited a dominant negative mutant of PcrA/UvrD in which a glutamate in the Walker B motif is substituted to allow DNA and ATP binding, but not hydrolysis and concomitant DNA translocation (Brosh and Matson, 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: Studies in many Additional Strand Catalytic E (ASCE)-class NTPases identify the glutamate residue in the Walker B motif as the catalytic base which accepts a proton from water, thereby promoting nucleophilic attack at the γ-phosphate and enabling ATP hydrolysis.
source: Studies in many Additional Strand Catalytic E (ASCE)-class NTPases identify this residue as the catalytic base which accepts a proton from water, thereby promoting nucleophilic attack at the γ-phosphate and enabling ATP hydrolysis (Thomsen and Berger, 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: Substitution of the glutamate residue in the Walker B motif with glutamine prevents ATP hydrolysis, trapping the enzyme in an ATP-bound or transition-like state.
source: Substitution of this glutamate residue with glutamine prevents ATP hydrolysis, trapping the enzyme in an ATP-bound or transition-like state (Hirano and Hirano, 2004; Soultanas et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: Induction of PcrA-E224Q from an ectopic locus in otherwise wild-type cells caused severe growth defects which became most apparent as the cells entered exponential phase.
source: Induction of PcrA-E224Q from an ectopic locus in otherwise wild-type cells caused severe growth defects which became most apparent as the cells entered exponential phase (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The growth defect caused by PcrA-E224Q was not apparent when wild type PcrA was expressed from the same locus.
source: This defect was not apparent when wild type PcrA was expressed from the same locus and is therefore due to the E224Q mutation as opposed to the effects of overexpression per se or the elevated cellular PcrA concentration that results.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The growth defect caused by PcrA-E224Q is due to the E224Q mutation as opposed to the effects of overexpression per se or the elevated cellular PcrA concentration that results.
source: This defect was not apparent when wild type PcrA was expressed from the same locus and is therefore due to the E224Q mutation as opposed to the effects of overexpression per se or the elevated cellular PcrA concentration that results.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the Results section based on the growth curve data.

claim: Delaying the induction of PcrA-E224Q until the onset of exponential phase resulted in a much smaller effect, presumably because a lower concentration of mutant PcrA had accumulated in early exponential phase.
source: Interestingly, delaying the induction of PcrA-E224Q until the onset of exponential phase (see Materials and methods and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A for details) resulted in a much smaller effect, presumably because a lower concentration of mutant PcrA had accumulated in early exponential phase.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The toxic effect of dysfunctional PcrA is mainly felt during rapid growth.
source: This may suggest that the toxic effect of dysfunctional PcrA is mainly felt during rapid growth.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the Results section based on the growth curve data.

claim: Removal of the CTD from the dominant negative mutant did not relieve the toxicity observed.
source: Removal of the CTD from the dominant negative mutant did not relieve the toxicity we observed.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section.

claim: PcrA-E224Q lacking the CTD can still interact weakly with RNAP.
source: This could indicate that PcrA-E224Q lacking the CTD can still interact weakly with RNAP (as we have discussed above) or that the toxic effect we observe arises from another role of this multifunctional enzyme that does not require the CTD.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the Results section based on the toxicity data and previous discussion of weak interactions.

claim: The toxic effect of PcrA-E224Q may arise from another role of this multifunctional enzyme that does not require the CTD.
source: This could indicate that PcrA-E224Q lacking the CTD can still interact weakly with RNAP (as we have discussed above) or that the toxic effect we observe arises from another role of this multifunctional enzyme that does not require the CTD.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the Results section based on the toxicity data.

claim: Removal of mfd had no substantial effects on the growth defect caused by PcrA-E224Q.
source: We also tested whether removal of mfd (that has been shown to counteract PcrA essentiality [Moreno-Del Alamo et al., 2020]) could relieve the mutant's toxicity but found that the deletion had no substantial effects on the growth defect (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Wild-type PcrA overexpression did not alter relative R-loop levels.
source: Wild-type PcrA overexpression did not alter relative R-loop levels, whereas overexpression of the E224Q mutant led to a significant increase (~2.7 fold).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by dot blot data shown in Figure 6D–E.

claim: Overexpression of the E224Q mutant led to a significant increase (~2.7 fold) in relative R-loop levels.
source: Wild-type PcrA overexpression did not alter relative R-loop levels, whereas overexpression of the E224Q mutant led to a significant increase (~2.7 fold).

claim: The increase in R-loop levels caused by PcrA-E224Q overexpression is comparable to the effect of deleting known R-loop suppression factors from bacterial cells such as rnhC or inhibiting rho using BCM in E. coli.

claim: The free CTD inhibited the interaction between full length PcrA and RNAP based on in vitro TEC supershifts and ex vivo pulldown assays.

claim: Overexpression of the CTD in cells should block endogenous wild-type PcrA from being recruited by RNAP.

claim: The increase in R-loop levels caused by WT CTD overexpression approached the levels associated with an rnhC deletion strain.

claim: The PcrA:TEC complex was still formed between the CTD (which lacks the helicase domains) and the TEC.
source: The complex was unaffected by removal of the upstream or downstream DNA duplex from the TEC, was still formed between the CTD (which lacks the helicase domains) and the TEC, and was not formed when a truncated form of PcrA lacking the CTD was used.

claim: The PcrA:TEC complex was not formed when a truncated form of PcrA lacking the CTD was used.
source: The complex was unaffected by removal of the upstream or downstream DNA duplex from the TEC, was still formed between the CTD (which lacks the helicase domains) and the TEC, and was not formed when a truncated form of PcrA lacking the CTD was used.

source: HDX-MS analysis confirmed that RNAP interacted with a face of the PcrA Tudor fold that is frequently observed to form protein interactions in other systems (Musselman et al., 2012; Ruthenburg et al., 2007).

source: The site for this PcrA-CTD interaction on the RNA polymerase was identified as a short peptide motif in the β subunit that sits within the SI1 domain.

source: This interaction site is distinct from that bound by the TC-NER factor Mfd, which also engages with the beta subunit via a Tudor domain but at the β1 domain.

source: The short peptide motif to which PcrA binds is highly conserved within Bacillus-like SI1 domains but does not obviously align with β subunit sequences from more distantly related organisms.

claim: Bioinformatics revealed that the same motif is present widely in bacterial RNAPs, but that its positioning within the SI1 domain is different depending on the lineage.
source: This paradox was resolved using bioinformatics, which revealed that the same motif is present widely in bacterial RNAPs, but that its positioning within the SI1 domain is different depending on the lineage.

source: Relative to other more universal features in RpoB sequences, the interaction motif appears later in B. subtilis-like domains (which are representative of Firmicutes) than it does in E. coli-like domains (which are representative of Proteobacteria; see Figure 2—figure supplement 2).

claim: Examples of bacterial RpoB species were found for which no clear helicase-interaction motif was present in the SI1 domain.
source: Note, however, that we did find examples of bacterial RpoB species for which we could find no clear helicase-interaction motif present in the SI1 domain.

claim: Sequence searches for the helicase interaction motif revealed the presence of the same motif in other known PcrA-interacting proteins, including UvrB, YxaL, and YwhK.
source: Our sequence searches proved rewarding as they revealed the presence of the same motif in other known PcrA-interacting proteins, including UvrB, YxaL, and YwhK.

source: Moreover, this helicase interaction motif is also present in several poorly characterised proteins which might be previously unidentified interaction partners for PcrA.

claim: Where a structure is available, the motif always adopts a beta-hairpin with the highly conserved TGE triad protruding towards the solvent.
source: Where a structure is available, the motif always adopts a beta-hairpin with the highly conserved TGE triad protruding towards the solvent.

claim: RNAP and UvrB might compete in the cell for the PcrA/UvrD helicase.
source: The corollary of our observation that RNAP and UvrB employ the same structural element to recruit PcrA is that they might compete in the cell for the PcrA/UvrD helicase.

source: This idea is supported directly by competition pulldown assays and is consistent with previous work in which the PcrA/UvrD CTD was shown to be important for interaction with both RNAP and UvrB (Manelyte et al., 2009; Sanders et al., 2017).

claim: The helicase interaction motif was absent from some known PcrA partners including the mismatch repair factor MutL.
source: However, the helicase interaction motif was absent from some known PcrA partners including the mismatch repair factor MutL.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion.

source: This is in agreement with recent work which showed that MutL binds and activates PcrA/UvrD via the 2B domain, rather than the CTD (Ordabayev et al., 2018; Ordabayev et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

claim: PcrA/UvrD, along with ppGpp, has been suggested to participate in an Mfd-independent transcription-coupled DNA repair pathway.
source: PcrA/UvrD, along with ppGpp, has been suggested to participate in an Mfd-independent transcription-coupled DNA repair pathway (Epshtein et al., 2014; Pani and Nudler, 2017).

source: In this pathway, UvrD is thought to promote backtracking of RNAP stalled at bulky DNA lesions and then recruits NER factors including UvrB to repair the damage.

source: We find here that RNAP and UvrB compete for PcrA interaction using the same conserved motif, meaning it is unclear how UvrB would be recruited to the UvrD:RNAP complex.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion.

claim: The role of UvrD in promoting strand-specific repair of DNA lesions remains controversial because a genome-wide analysis of cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers showed no evidence for Mfd-independent TC-NER.
source: Moreover, the role of UvrD in promoting strand-specific repair of DNA lesions remains controversial because a genome-wide analysis of cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers showed no evidence for Mfd-independent TC-NER and also that the levels of ppGpp do not change the repair rate in E. coli (Adebali et al., 2017a; Adebali et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

claim: The levels of ppGpp do not change the repair rate in E. coli.
source: Moreover, the role of UvrD in promoting strand-specific repair of DNA lesions remains controversial because a genome-wide analysis of cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers showed no evidence for Mfd-independent TC-NER and also that the levels of ppGpp do not change the repair rate in E. coli (Adebali et al., 2017a; Adebali et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

source: The HDX-MS data with full-length PcrA showed that the core helicase domains interact with multiple elements surrounding the RNA and DNA exit channels, for instance the β-flap tip and the N-terminal part of the β′ subunit, as has been shown previously by crosslinking-MS data for the complex between E. coli RNAP and UvrD (Epshtein et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a summary of findings stated in the Discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: The HDX-MS data also identified an interaction with the SI1 domain which can be assigned to the PcrA CTD.
source: Our HDX-MS data also identified an interaction with the SI1 domain which we can assign to the PcrA CTD.
evidence: This is a summary of findings stated in the Discussion.

source: The exit channels for nucleic acids are distant from the SI1 domain, but the long linker between the helicase core and the CTD is sufficiently long to accommodate both interaction patches.

source: Interestingly, the length of this linker varies in different PcrA orthologues in a manner that reflects the distance between the RNAP exit channels and SI1 domains in each system.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion.

claim: It is possible to build a speculative physical model which satisfies both the HDX data and the crosslinking study of the E. coli system.
source: The precise details of the PcrA-RNAP interaction will await a high-resolution structure of the complex, but it is possible to build a speculative physical model which satisfies both our own HDX data and the crosslinking study of the E. coli system. (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by a model shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The involvement of the main body of the helicase in RNAP interactions may help to explain the phenotypes associated with CTD deletion.
source: The involvement of the main body of the helicase in RNAP interactions may also help to explain the phenotypes associated with CTD deletion.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion.

claim: Given the apparently key role played by the PcrA/UvrD CTD as a protein interaction hub, it is surprising that its complete removal has little effect on nucleotide excision repair or replication-transcription conflicts in E. coli.
source: Given the apparently key role played by the PcrA/UvrD CTD as a protein interaction hub, it is surprising that its complete removal has little effect on nucleotide excision repair or replication-transcription conflicts in E. coli (Merrikh et al., 2015; Sanders et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

claim: In B. subtilis where PcrA is recruited to highly transcribed regions of the genome to facilitate replication through active transcription units, the CTD seems to be dispensable.
source: Similarly, in B. subtilis where PcrA is recruited to highly transcribed regions of the genome to facilitate replication through active transcription units, the CTD seems to be dispensable (Merrikh et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by a citation.

source: A possible explanation lies in the fact that PcrA-RNAP association also involves the main body of the helicase including the core motor domain 2A, whose activity is largely unchanged by removal of the CTD. It is possible that residual weak interactions allow PcrA helicase core to function effectively in the absence of the CTD in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the Discussion.

source: However, it should also be acknowledged that stable interactions between the PcrA helicase core and RNAP cannot be detected between purified proteins (this and previous work Gwynn et al., 2013; Sanders et al., 2017), and consequently, we did not pursue HDX-MS experiments between these constructs.

source: Therefore, at least in vitro, the presence of the CTD appears to facilitate binding of the core helicase domains near the RNA exit channels.

source: Moreover, our observation of increased DNA-RNA hybrids in cells in which the free CTD is overexpressed provides a direct link between the RNAP binding function of the CTD and R-loop metabolism.

source: The location of the helicase core close to the RNA exit channel led us to consider roles for PcrA in manipulating the transcript.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion.

source: Due to the enzyme's inability to translocate on RNA or to unwind duplex RNAs, we hypothesised that PcrA might act to unwind DNA/RNA hybrids that are formed upstream of the transcription bubble.

source: This idea was supported by experiments in Bacillus subtilis showing that R-loop concentration in cells was increased by two- to threefold by overexpressing dominant negative PcrA or free CTD (which blocks PcrA-RNAP interaction).
evidence: This is a summary of findings stated in the Discussion.

source: This strongly suggests that an activity of wild-type PcrA, which is dependent upon interactions made by its CTD, is important for suppressing R-loops.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the Discussion based on the experimental findings.

claim: PcrA decreases R-loop levels in cells by unwinding RNA-DNA hybrids that form behind the transcription elongation complex.
source: Although out work does not establish the mechanism by which PcrA decreases R-loop levels in cells, we hypothesise that it does so by unwinding RNA-DNA hybrids that form behind the transcription elongation complex (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the Discussion and supported by a model shown in Figure 7.

claim: The well-documented 3′>5′ polarity of PcrA/UvrD helicase, together with its inability to move along RNA strands, suggests two possible working models for the unwinding of R-loops.
source: The well-documented 3′>5′ polarity of PcrA/UvrD helicase (Bird et al., 1998), together with its inability to move along RNA strands, suggests two possible working models for the unwinding of R-loops.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: In the 'co-directional' model, the helicase translocates on the template strand and in the same direction as the RNA polymerase, unwinding R-loops as they form.
source: In the first 'co-directional' model, the helicase translocates on the template strand and in the same direction as the RNA polymerase, unwinding R-loops as they form.
evidence: This is a proposed model stated in the Discussion and illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: In the 'backtracking model', the helicase translocates on the non-template strand of the R-loop and in the opposite direction to transcription, indirectly unwinding the DNA/RNA hybrid by making the polymerase backtrack.
source: Another possibility (the 'backtracking model') is that the helicase translocates on the non-template strand of the R-loop and in the opposite direction to transcription, indirectly unwinding the DNA/RNA hybrid by making the polymerase backtrack (Epshtein et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a proposed model stated in the Discussion and illustrated in Figure 7, supported by a citation.

claim: In the backtracking model, the lid domain of RNAP, rather than the helicase itself, would act as the 'ploughshare' to separate the two strands.
source: In this scenario the lid domain of RNAP, rather than the helicase itself, would act as the 'ploughshare' to separate the two strands.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as part of the backtracking model.

source: We favour the first model because our HDX protection data places the 2A domain of PcrA (which is at the front of the moving helicase) in direct contact with the RNA exit region, suggesting that the helicase translocates towards the RNA polymerase.

claim: The close contact between PcrA and RNAP suggested by the data could mean that R-loops are unwound as they are formed at the exit channels, rather than being targeted after they have extended behind the TEC.
source: Indeed, the close contact between PcrA and RNAP suggested by our data could mean that R-loops are unwound as they are formed at the exit channels, rather than being targeted after they have extended behind the TEC.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the Discussion based on the HDX-MS data.

claim: Previous observations of UvrD-dependent backtracking of RNAP are more consistent with the backtracking model.
source: However, we also note that previous observations of UvrD-dependent backtracking of RNAP are more consistent with the second backtracking model (Epshtein et al., 2014; Sanders et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

claim: The role of the CTD is to target the helicase activity to its physiological substrate in vivo (i.e. to increase the local concentration of PcrA near R-loops), rather than to catalytically activate the DNA motor protein in response to its engagement with RNAP.
source: In these models, we propose that the role of the CTD is simply to target the helicase activity to its physiological substrate in vivo (i.e. to increase the local concentration of PcrA near R-loops), rather than to catalytically activate the DNA motor protein in response to its engagement with RNAP.
evidence: This is a proposed model stated in the Discussion.

source: This view is consistent with our observation that free CTD can block R-loop suppression through dominant negative effects on wild-type PcrA, and also with previously published work in which we have observed only moderate effects of adding RNAP and/or removing the CTD on the ATPase and helicase activities of PcrA (Gwynn et al., 2013; Velankar et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

claim: Only moderate effects of adding RNAP and/or removing the CTD on the ATPase and helicase activities of PcrA have been observed in previously published work.
source: This view is consistent with our observation that free CTD can block R-loop suppression through dominant negative effects on wild-type PcrA, and also with previously published work in which we have observed only moderate effects of adding RNAP and/or removing the CTD on the ATPase and helicase activities of PcrA (Gwynn et al., 2013; Velankar et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

source: A role for PcrA in suppressing R-loops can explain its function in alleviating replication:transcription conflicts as well as why the helicase is enriched at highly transcribed rRNA and tRNA genes that have been shown to be prone to R-loop formation in yeast and human cells (Boubakri et al., 2010; Chan et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2017; Guy et al., 2009; Merrikh et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

claim: The helicase is enriched at highly transcribed rRNA and tRNA genes that have been shown to be prone to R-loop formation in yeast and human cells.
source: A role for PcrA in suppressing R-loops can explain its function in alleviating replication:transcription conflicts as well as why the helicase is enriched at highly transcribed rRNA and tRNA genes that have been shown to be prone to R-loop formation in yeast and human cells (Boubakri et al., 2010; Chan et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2017; Guy et al., 2009; Merrikh et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

source: An R-loop suppression function might also explain why loss of PcrA leads to hyper-recombination and the formation of RecFOR- and RecA-dependent toxic recombination intermediates (Arthur and Lloyd, 1980; Moreno-Del Alamo et al., 2020; Petit and Ehrlich, 2002; Veaute et al., 2005).

source: The displaced ssDNA within an unresolved R-loop may act as a 'frustrated' substrate for ssDNA gap repair, resulting in RecA recruitment and strand exchange but failing to be processed correctly into repaired products because of the presence of the R-loop and TEC.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the Discussion.

source: Finally, a very recent study involving depletion of PcrA in rnhB, rnhC, and dinG backgrounds led to the conclusion that PcrA alleviates replication-transcription conflicts, with biochemical analysis supporting the idea (broadly similar to that presented here) that the helicase activity of PcrA acts to unwind and remove R-loops in concert with R-loop nucleases (Moreno-Del Álamo et al., 2021).
